body.statement: The map \(P\mapsto P_{\mathrm{obs}}\) is injective for \(\{(f_x,q_x):x\in\mathcal X\}\) over \(\mathcal M\). On a common neighborhood of zero, \(\left.\partial_t\log F_x(u,t)\right|_{t=0}=\widehat f_x'(u)/\widehat f_x(u)+\phi_2'(0)=\widehat f_x'(u)/\widehat f_x(u)\), because \(\phi_2(0)=1\) and \(\phi_2'(0)=iE_P[U_2]=0\). Together with \(\widehat f_x(0)=1\), this derivative identity uniquely fixes the latent translation without a normalization on \(U_1\). Moreover, \(\widehat q_x(u)=\widehat f_x(u)G_x(u,0)/F_x(u,0)\). Compact support makes both recovered transforms entire, so the local formulas determine \(f_x\) and \(q_x\) globally even when either error transform has an open zero set away from zero.
body.justification: It makes the causal ratio a functional of the observed marked replicate law without symmetry or global nonvanishing.
body.gap: Theorem 1 of Capitao-Miniconi, Gassiat, and Lehéricy gives the probability-channel cocycle; it does not state the outcome-weighted signed channel or its compatibility with the recovered probability channel.
body.consumer: It supplies the law-level target set for honest-band inversion in two-recall exposure studies.
body.proof_tex:
Fix two laws \(P^{(0)},P^{(1)}\in\mathcal M\) inducing the same observed law, and fix \(x\in\mathcal X\).  By \(\mathrm{ass{:}strata}\), \(P^{(k)}(X=x)\ge p_{\min}>0\), so both conditional channels \(F_x\) and \(G_x\) are determined by the common observed law.

We first derive, rather than assume, a common nonvanishing neighborhood.  By \(\mathrm{ass{:}error\text{-}moment}\) and the enlarged range \(q_e>1\), the power-mean inequality gives, for \(j\in\{1,2\}\),
\[
 E_{P^{(k)}}|U_j|
 \le \{E_{P^{(k)}}|U_j|^{q_e}\}^{1/q_e}
 \le M_e^{1/q_e}.
 \tag{1}
\]
Since \(|e^{iv}-1|\le |v|\) for real \(v\),
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 |\phi_j^{(k)}(t)|
 &\ge 1-|\phi_j^{(k)}(t)-1|\\
 &\ge 1-E_{P^{(k)}}|e^{itU_j}-1|\\
 &\ge 1-|t|E_{P^{(k)}}|U_j|\\
 &\ge 1-|t|M_e^{1/q_e}.
 \end{aligned}
 \tag{2}
\]
Thus, with
\[
 \nu_*=(2M_e^{1/q_e})^{-1},\qquad c_*=\frac12,
 \tag{3}
\]
one has \(|\phi_j^{(k)}(t)|\ge c_*\) whenever \(|t|\le\nu_*\), uniformly in \(j\), \(k\), and the law.  No separate spectral-modulus condition has been used.

Set
\[
 \delta=\min\left\{\nu_*,\frac{1}{4B_A}\right\}>0.
 \tag{4}
\]
Assumption \(\mathrm{ass{:}compact\text{-}dose}\) says that \(|A|\le B_A\) almost surely.  Hence, for \(|v|\le2\delta\),
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 |\widehat f_x^{(k)}(v)-1|
 &\le \int_{\mathcal A}|e^{iva}-1|f_x^{(k)}(a)\,da\\
 &\le |v|\int_{\mathcal A}|a|f_x^{(k)}(a)\,da\\
 &\le B_A|v|\le\frac12,
 \end{aligned}
 \tag{5}
\]
and therefore \(|\widehat f_x^{(k)}(v)|\ge1/2\).  If \(|u|,|t|\le\delta\), then \(|u+t|\le2\delta\); equations (2), (4), and (5), followed by \(\mathrm{lem{:}factorization}\), yield
\[
 |F_x(u,t)|
 =|\widehat f_x^{(k)}(u+t)\phi_1^{(k)}(u)\phi_2^{(k)}(t)|
 \ge \frac12c_*^2>0.
 \tag{6}
\]

The compact support of \(f_x^{(k)}\) permits differentiation of \(\widehat f_x^{(k)}\), while (1) permits differentiation of \(\phi_2^{(k)}\) at zero by dominated convergence.  Differentiating the factorization in \(\mathrm{lem{:}factorization}\), dividing by (6), and using \(\phi_2^{(k)}(0)=1\), we obtain, for \(|u|\le\delta\),
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 D_x(u)
 &:=\frac{\left.\partial_tF_x(u,t)\right|_{t=0}}{F_x(u,0)}\\
 &=\frac{(\widehat f_x^{(k)})'(u)}{\widehat f_x^{(k)}(u)}
   +\frac{(\phi_2^{(k)})'(0)}{\phi_2^{(k)}(0)}.
 \end{aligned}
 \tag{7}
\]
Equivalently, (7) is the asserted logarithmic derivative for any local continuous branch of the logarithm, whose existence follows from (6).  Assumption \(\mathrm{ass{:}center\text{-}two}\) and dominated differentiation give
\[
 (\phi_2^{(k)})'(0)=iE_{P^{(k)}}[U_2]=0.
 \tag{8}
\]
The function \(D_x\) is determined solely by the common observed channel.  Equations (7)--(8) therefore imply
\[
 (\widehat f_x^{(k)})'(u)=D_x(u)\widehat f_x^{(k)}(u),
 \qquad \widehat f_x^{(k)}(0)=1.
 \tag{9}
\]
Because the denominator is nonzero by (5), the ratio
\(R(u)=\widehat f_x^{(1)}(u)/\widehat f_x^{(0)}(u)\) is differentiable on \([-\delta,\delta]\).  Equation (9) gives \(R'(u)=0\), and normalization gives \(R(0)=1\).  Consequently
\[
 \widehat f_x^{(1)}(u)=\widehat f_x^{(0)}(u),
 \qquad |u|\le\delta.
 \tag{10}
\]
This calculation never differentiates \(\phi_1\), so it imposes no location normalization on \(U_1\).

We next extend (10) globally without assuming global nonvanishing of either error transform.  Compact support gives, for every complex \(z\),
\[
 \sum_{r=0}^{\infty}\frac{|z|^r}{r!}
 \int_{\mathcal A}|a|^rf_x^{(k)}(a)\,da
 \le e^{B_A|z|}.
 \tag{11}
\]
Tonelli's theorem and (11) justify termwise integration of the exponential series, so
\[
 \widehat f_x^{(k)}(z)
 =\sum_{r=0}^{\infty}\frac{(iz)^r}{r!}
   \int_{\mathcal A}a^rf_x^{(k)}(a)\,da,
 \qquad z\in\mathbb C.
 \tag{12}
\]
Thus each transform is entire.  The difference of the transforms in (10) is zero on a real neighborhood of zero, so all of its real derivatives at zero vanish.  Those derivatives equal the complex derivatives supplied by (12); hence every coefficient of its globally convergent power series is zero.  It follows that
\[
 \widehat f_x^{(1)}(z)=\widehat f_x^{(0)}(z),
 \qquad z\in\mathbb C.
 \tag{13}
\]

For the marked channel, put \(t=0\) in the two identities of \(\mathrm{lem{:}factorization}\).  Since \(F_x(u,0)\ne0\) for \(|u|\le\delta\), division is legitimate and gives, under either candidate law,
\[
 \widehat q_x^{(k)}(u)
 =\widehat f_x^{(k)}(u)\frac{G_x(u,0)}{F_x(u,0)},
 \qquad |u|\le\delta.
 \tag{14}
\]
The right-hand side is the same for \(k=0,1\) by the common observed law and (10).  Hence the two marked transforms agree locally.  Assumptions \(\mathrm{ass{:}consistency}\) and \(\mathrm{ass{:}bounded\text{-}outcome}\) imply \(|Y|\le B_Y\) almost surely and therefore \(|m_x(a)|\le B_Y\) for \(f_x(a)\,da\)-almost every \(a\).  Since \(q_x=m_xf_x\),
\[
 |q_x(a)|\le B_Yf_x(a)\quad\text{almost everywhere},
 \qquad \operatorname{supp}(q_x)\subseteq\mathcal A,
 \qquad \|q_x\|_1\le B_Y.
 \tag{15}
\]
Replacing \(f_x^{(k)}\) by \(q_x^{(k)}\) and the right side of (11) by \(B_Ye^{B_A|z|}\) proves that \(\widehat q_x^{(k)}\) is entire.  The power-series argument used for (13), now starting from the local equality implied by (14), yields
\[
 \widehat q_x^{(1)}(z)=\widehat q_x^{(0)}(z),
 \qquad z\in\mathbb C.
 \tag{16}
\]

For completeness, we verify that equality of transforms identifies the underlying functions.  Let \(h\) be the difference of the two candidate \(f_x\)'s or of the two candidate \(q_x\)'s.  Equations (13) and (16) give \(\widehat h(t)=0\) for every real \(t\), while compact support and (15) give \(h\in L^1(\mathbb R)\).  For \(\epsilon>0\), define
\[
 g_\epsilon(v)=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-1/2}e^{-v^2/(2\epsilon)}
 =\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-itv}e^{-\epsilon t^2/2}\,dt.
 \tag{17}
\]
Fubini's theorem applies because \(h\in L^1\) and the Gaussian multiplier is integrable.  Therefore
\[
 (h*g_\epsilon)(a)
 =\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-ita}\widehat h(t)
       e^{-\epsilon t^2/2}\,dt=0.
 \tag{18}
\]
Translation is continuous in \(L^1\): it is immediate for compactly supported step functions, and the general case follows by approximating \(h\) in \(L^1\), because translation preserves the \(L^1\)-norm.  Consequently
\[
 \|h*g_\epsilon-h\|_1
 \le\int_{\mathbb R}g_\epsilon(v)
       \|h(\mathord\cdot-v)-h\|_1\,dv\longrightarrow0.
 \tag{19}
\]
Indeed, on a fixed neighborhood of zero the integrand in (19) is uniformly small by translation continuity, outside that neighborhood it is at most \(2\|h\|_1\), and the Gaussian mass there tends to zero.  Equations (18)--(19) imply \(h=0\) almost everywhere.

Finally, \(\mathrm{ass{:}f\text{-}sobolev}\), \(\mathrm{ass{:}q\text{-}sobolev}\), and the enlarged range \(\beta>1/2\) select unique continuous representatives.  In fact, for either difference \(h\), Cauchy--Schwarz gives
\[
 \int_{\mathbb R}|\widehat h(t)|\,dt
 \le
 \left\{\int_{\mathbb R}(1+t^2)^\beta|\widehat h(t)|^2\,dt\right\}^{1/2}
 \left\{\int_{\mathbb R}(1+t^2)^{-\beta}\,dt\right\}^{1/2}<\infty.
 \tag{20}
\]
Fourier inversion therefore supplies a continuous representative, and a continuous function that is zero almost everywhere is zero everywhere.  Thus \(f_x^{(0)}=f_x^{(1)}\) and \(q_x^{(0)}=q_x^{(1)}\).  Since \(x\) was arbitrary, the common observed law identifies all \(\{(f_x,q_x):x\in\mathcal X\}\).  Equations (2)--(3) show that this conclusion permits open spectral zero sets away from zero and requires no separately assumed local modulus.
